problem: Instruction-following navigation in unknown indoor environments typically requires explicit semantic models or maps to represent instruction meaning; hand-built semantic representations are brittle and do not scale to varied verbal expressions.
motivation: Robots should follow natural verbal instructions without prior knowledge of the environment. Feeding word vectors directly into a neural network lets the robot learn instruction-to-action mapping from human demonstrations instead of engineering semantic models.
key_idea: A recursive neural network takes word-vector-encoded verbal instructions plus laser range finder data and outputs control velocities, trained on human-teleoperated navigation records.
insight: Only the abstract was available, so no ablations can be cited. The abstract suggests that distributed word vectors can replace explicit semantic models and that end-to-end imitation from human demonstrations can ground language into velocity control.
method: Instruction encoding: verbal instructions are converted to word vectors and fed directly into the network, with no explicit semantic model.
Recursive neural network: combines the instruction representation with laser range finder observations.
Control output: the network outputs control velocities for the mobile robot.
Training: imitation learning from human-controlled navigation records across varied instructions.

setting.backbone: Recursive neural network with word vectors (trained from scratch, per abstract)
setting.training_data: Human-controlled navigation records (teleoperated demonstrations) paired with verbal instructions; scale not stated in abstract
setting.observation: Laser range finder data plus verbal instruction text (no vision)
setting.privileged: none (no prior knowledge of the environment)

results: The abstract reports qualitatively that the robot successfully navigates to goal positions in both simulation and real-world experiments without prior environment knowledge. No numbers or baselines are given.
